title: “Here Am I. Send Me.”
paragraphs:
“Here Am I. Send Me.”
The Four Words That Can Change an Ordinary Life Into a Story God Uses for Eternity
There are moments in life when everything changes, not because our circumstances change, but because we finally see God for who He truly is.

Most people imagine their greatest spiritual moment would happen on a mountain, during a worship service, or after receiving an answer to prayer. Yet one of the most powerful transformations recorded in Scripture began in a moment of grief, uncertainty, and national instability.
Isaiah tells us:
"In the year that King Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up..." (Isaiah 6:1)
A king had died. An era had ended. The future felt uncertain.
Many of us know that feeling.
The diagnosis came.
The marriage struggled.
The business failed.
The dream collapsed.
Someone we loved left.
Something we trusted disappeared.
And then, in the middle of the shaking, God revealed Himself.
Isaiah did not begin with a mission.
He began with a vision.
Before God sent him anywhere, God showed him who He was.
The prophet saw the Lord exalted above every earthly throne. The seraphim cried out continually:

קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ
Qādōsh, Qādōsh, Qādōsh
“Holy, Holy, Holy.”
The repetition is not accidental.
In Hebrew, repetition intensifies meaning. Scripture never says God is merely loving, loving, loving or powerful, powerful, powerful.
But it does say:
“Holy, Holy, Holy.”
God is utterly separate from sin.
Perfectly pure.
Perfectly righteous.
Perfectly glorious.
Isaiah's response was immediate.
Not excitement.
Not confidence.
Not self-promotion.
Not ambition.
He cried:

אוֹי־לִי כִּי־נִדְמֵיתִי
Oy-li ki nidmeiti
“Woe is me! For I am ruined!” (Isaiah 6:5)
The closer a person gets to the holiness of God, the less impressed they become with themselves.
Isaiah was already a prophet.
Already respected.
Already used by God.
Yet standing before divine holiness exposed what religion often hides.
His need for grace.
This is where the Gospel begins.
Not with human achievement.
Not with self-improvement.
Not with trying harder.
The Gospel begins when sinners realize they cannot save themselves.
Isaiah confessed:
“I am a man of unclean lips.”
Then something extraordinary happened.
One of the seraphim took a burning coal from the altar and touched his mouth.
The angel declared:
“Your guilt is taken away and your sin atoned for.” (Isaiah 6:7)
The Hebrew language is beautiful here.
The phrase translated “atoned for” comes from the root כָּפַר (kaphar), carrying the idea of covering, cleansing, and reconciliation.
Isaiah did not cleanse himself.
God provided cleansing.
Isaiah did not remove his guilt.
God removed it.
Isaiah did not earn forgiveness.
God gave it.
Thousands of years later, this scene would point toward an even greater reality.
The coal came from the altar of sacrifice.
The cross became the ultimate altar.
The blood of Jesus Christ accomplished forever what every sacrifice anticipated.
As the Apostle Paul wrote:
“God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
This is why Christianity is different from every system built upon human effort.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself and come.”
The Gospel says, “Come, and Christ will clean you.”
The Gospel does not say, “Become worthy.”
The Gospel says, “Jesus is worthy.”
The Gospel does not say, “Fix your life first.”
The Gospel says, “Trust the One who gave His life for you.”
Only after Isaiah encountered God's holiness and received God's grace did the famous moment occur.
Then Isaiah heard the voice of the Lord:
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for Us?”
Notice something remarkable.
God already knew the answer.
The question was never about God's information.
The question was about Isaiah's surrender.
Then came one of the most powerful responses in all of Scripture:

הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Hineni, shelacheni.
“Here am I. Send me.”
The word הִנְנִי (Hineni) means far more than simply “here I am.”
It carries the sense of complete availability.
Complete readiness.
Complete surrender.
It is the language of someone placing their entire life into God's hands.
Not “Here is part of me.”
Not “Here is my Sunday self.”
Not “Here is my spare time.”
But “All of me belongs to You.”
This is the deeper meaning of Isaiah 6:8.
It is not primarily about missions.
It is not primarily about ministry.
It is not primarily about a career calling.
It is the response of a heart overwhelmed by the holiness of God, transformed by the grace of God, and surrendered to the purposes of God.
Isaiah was not volunteering to earn acceptance.
He was responding because he had already received mercy.
That changes everything.
Many people spend their entire lives asking, “What does God want me to do?”
The greater question may be:
“Has my heart reached the place where I can honestly say, ‘Hineni’?”
Because God is still asking.
Not only from pulpits.
Not only from missionaries.
Not only from pastors.
But from fathers.
Mothers.
Students.
Business owners.
Employees.
Retirees.
Young believers.
Seasoned saints.
He is still asking who will carry His truth into a confused world.
Who will stand for Christ when compromise is easier.
Who will forgive when bitterness feels justified.
Who will love when hatred seems popular.
Who will speak hope where despair dominates.
Who will point people to Jesus instead of themselves.
The world does not merely need more opinions.
It needs more surrendered hearts.
Perhaps that is why Isaiah's words continue to echo across centuries.
Because every believer eventually reaches the same crossroads.
Will we protect our comfort?
Or will we trust the One who saved us?
Will we live for temporary applause?
Or eternal purpose?
Will we remain spectators?
Or become participants in God's redemptive story?
The greatest tragedy is not failure.
The greatest tragedy is hearing God's call and never responding.
Imagine standing before Christ one day and realizing how many opportunities were missed because fear had the final word.
But imagine something greater.
Imagine hearing, by God's grace, “Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Imagine discovering that every act of obedience mattered.
Every prayer mattered.
Every sacrifice mattered.
Every conversation mattered.
Every moment of surrender mattered.
Because Jesus has always specialized in rewriting stories.
He rewrote Peter's failure.
He rewrote Paul's violence.
He rewrote Mary's shame.
He rewrote the thief's final moments.
He rewrote countless broken lives throughout history.
And He is still rewriting lives today.
Maybe you are reading this carrying regret.
Maybe you have chapters you wish nobody knew about.
Maybe your past feels heavier than your future.
The message of Isaiah 6 is not that God uses perfect people.
The message is that God cleanses imperfect people and then sends them.
Grace comes before the assignment.
Mercy comes before the mission.
Forgiveness comes before the sending.
That is why our theme remains true:

Your support helps us create more Christ-centered content, expand discipleship resources, reach more people with the Gospel, and continue pointing souls toward biblical truth. Supporting the work is not merely supporting content—it is participating in Gospel outreach that seeks to glorify God and make Christ known.
Before you leave, be honest with yourself.
If God asked today, “Whom shall I send?” would your answer be delayed by fear, excuses, comfort, or doubt?
Or could you say with Isaiah:
הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
“Here am I. Send me.”
The people God uses most are rarely the people who think they are qualified. They are the people who have seen His holiness, received His mercy, and simply said yes.
The God who cleansed Isaiah is still calling ordinary people into extraordinary obedience today.
